t: The approachable grandfather god of Kannur, worshipped by people of every background.
x: Muthappan means “grandfather” in Malayalam, and that is how he is approached: as a close, forgiving elder who is easy to talk to. He is worshipped as two forms of one deity, Thiruvappana and Vellatom, and is often linked with Shiva. His rit

t: A powerful form of Vishnu, remembered through the story of the devotee Palanthai Kannan.
x: Vishnumoorthi is one of the two main Vaishnava deities in Theyyam. Scholars note that Vaishnavism arrived late in Kerala’s folk worship, so Vishnumoorthi stands out in a tradition mostly shaped by Shaiva and Shakta forms. The deity is also

t: The god who answered a scholar’s pride with a question about equality.
x: Pottan is a form of the divine that speaks against caste discrimination. In many tellings he is understood as Shiva in the guise of a low-caste man. Pottan is a lively, colourful ritual and an important part of the cultural heritage of the

t: A fierce guardian linked to time, fate and Yama.
x: Gulikan is a powerful guardian worshipped in Kerala and, as Guliga, in the Tulu-speaking region of coastal Karnataka. He is linked in astrology with Shani and is understood as an aspect of Yama, the god of death. His shrines are usually sma

t: A fiery child guardian said to be the son of Shiva and Parvati.
x: Kuttichathan is a widely loved guardian figure in Malabar folklore. He is often described as a mischievous but powerful child of the gods. The Theyyam is also called Shasthappan and, because it is associated with the Kalakattu family, Kalak

t: The brotherly guardian who travelled with the goddess Poomala.
x: Poomaruthan is a god of North Malabar who is worshipped together with the goddess Poomala. His name joins “poo”, a flower, and “maruthan”, wind.

t: A learned woman who became a goddess, and one of the most graceful of all Theyyams.
x: Muchilot Bhagavathi is the family deity of the Vaniya community in North Malabar. Her shrines are traditionally numbered at 108, echoing the 108 Shiva temples of the Shivalaya Stotram. She is widely described as the most elaborate and beaut

t: A beloved goddess whom women pray to for safe childbirth.
x: Uchitta is a regional goddess of Kannur and Kasaragod who is much loved by women, who pray to her for a safe delivery. Her name is said to come from her loud voice, “uchathil” in Malayalam.

t: The goddess associated with epidemic disease, worshipped for healing.
x: Vasoorimala is a female deity of Kerala and the Kodagu region who is worshipped as a sub-deity in Bhadrakali and Shiva temples. “Vasoori” is the Malayalam word for smallpox, and her name means “garland of pox”. In the old understanding, peo

t: A goddess who crossed the sea and found a friend in a Muslim sailor.
x: Arya Poonkani is a goddess of North Malabar whose story links two faiths. She appears together with Bappiriyan, a sailor who is believed to have been a Muslim.

t: A fierce warrior goddess, honoured in several forms across the region.
x: Chamundi is the fierce, protective form of the goddess, worshipped in several local forms. Three well-known types are Madayil Chamundi, Rakta Chamundi and Kundora Chamundi. Chamundi shrines are often kept by ruling families and households a

t: The warrior Mandappan Chekavar, remembered as a hero and honoured as a god.
x: Kathivanoor Veeran is one of the most popular Theyyams of North Malabar. “Veeran” means hero. He is remembered as Mandappan Chekavar, a Thiyya warrior whose life and death are still told in the folklore of the Kolathunadu region.

t: A gifted man who learned to become a leopard, and was wronged for it.
x: Pulimaranja Thondachan is worshipped mainly by the Pulayar community of Kannur and Kasaragod. “Thondachan” is a word for grandfather in North Malabar. The name means the ancestor who vanished as a tiger.

t: A wronged sister and her children, who became deities after their death.
x: Kadangot Makkam is a woman of the North Malabar region who is worshipped as a goddess after being wronged. Her Theyyam is also called Makkappothi, or “Makkam and her children”.

t: A sailor who is believed to have been a Muslim, honoured in a Hindu ritual.
x: Bappiriyan is a Theyyam of the Mappila tradition. He is believed to be a Muslim merchant and sea captain and is remembered alongside the goddess Arya Poonkani. The pairing is often cited as an example of Hindu-Muslim harmony in Kerala.

t: A Theyyam of devotion and fire, remembered through the story of Narasimha and Prahlada.
x: Theechamundi is a fire-linked Theyyam that is connected in most accounts with Vishnu in his Narasimha form. Although the name carries “Chamundi”, which is usually a goddess, the tellings we have found centre on Vishnu and fire. Accounts dif

t: A fierce, dark form of the warrior goddess Chamundi.
x: Karimchamundi is one of the best-known Chamundi forms in North Malabar. “Kari” or “karim” means dark or black, so the name is usually understood as the dark Chamundi. Like the other forms, she is a fierce, protective mother goddess who is h

t: A protective mother goddess, loved by the women of the household.
x: Kurathi Amma is a much-loved goddess of North Malabar, worshipped in family homes, village groves and temples. “Kurathi” is a word for a woman of the hill people, and she is often understood as a form of Parvati, the daughter of the mountai

t: A devoted farmer who was lost in a forest fire and restored to life as a deity.
x: Kandanar Kelan is a Theyyam of North Malabar that remembers a farmer named Kelan. The name is explained as “the one found in the forest fire”. Tellings agree on the outline and differ in details, so please treat the following as a general s

t: A blind hunter god, honoured as the chief deity of many Thiyya families.
x: Vayanattu Kulavan is a major deity of North Malabar who appears as a hunter, and is the principal deity of many Thiyya families. Other communities also revere him. He is also called Adhitheeyan and Thondachan, which means ancestor.

t: The fierce wandering form of Shiva, who begs with a skull.
x: Bhairavan is the fierce, wandering form of Shiva, who is shown as an ascetic. He is the chief deity of the Paanan community, and members of the Malayan community also keep him. Folklore writers place him among the deities that need especial

t: The tiger deities of North Malabar, born to Shiva and Parvati in tiger form.
x: Puli Daivam, the tiger deities, are a family of Theyyams of North Malabar. “Puli” means tiger. Kerala Tourism lists several of them: Puliyoor Kali, Pulikarinkali, Pulikandan, Marapuli, Kandapuli and Pulimaruthan.

t: A healer of snakebite, honoured after he was killed out of envy.
x: Vishakandan is a rare Theyyam that remembers Kandan, a Thiyya man who was known for curing snakebites. “Visha” means poison. We have found only one source for the story, so please treat it as local tradition.

t: A goddess said to have risen from a sacrificial fire, and the main deity of many Kannur shrines.
x: Puthiya Bhagavathi is a goddess who is the main deity of many shrines in the Kannur region. She is generally identified with Bhadrakali, and Cheerumba Bhagavathi is regarded as her younger sister.

t: Theyyams that honour Muslim figures, kept by Hindu and Muslim communities together.
x: “Mappila” is the local word for the Muslims of the Malabar coast. Mappila Theyyams are Theyyams whose figures are Muslim: sailors, imams, a woman who worked in a palace kitchen, a magician. They are held mainly in Kasaragod district and par

t: A Muslim woman honoured as a goddess, who wears a headscarf and is sung to in Mappila songs.
x: Ummachi is one of the best-known female Mappila Theyyams. Hindus and Muslims both take part in the ritual, and it is often given as an example of how this tradition crosses the lines of caste and religion.

t: A guardian in a khaki uniform who keeps order beside the goddess Karinchamundi.
x: Police Theyyam is one of the most unusual Theyyams. The deity is a policeman, in a khaki uniform, who accompanies the goddess Karinchamundi as her bodyguard. Besides the face painting, the uniform is what makes it recognisable as a Theyyam.

t: The wild boar deity of the Tulu coast and Kasaragod, and the Theyyam closest to “Varaha”.
x: Panjuruli is a spirit deity shown as a wild boar, worshipped across the Tulu-speaking coast of Karnataka and in parts of Kasaragod. “Panji” means pig in Tulu. In Kerala it appears as a Theyyam, and a popular source calls it the Theyyam base

t: The Theyyam that stands for Lakshmana in a set of Ramayana-based Theyyams.
x: Angakkaran is one of three linked Theyyams based on the Ramayana. According to Kerala Tourism, Daivathar stands for Rama, Angakkaran for his brother Lakshmana, and Bappuran for Hanuman. They appear at a shrine whose festival includes more t

t: A Vaishnava Theyyam that stands for Rama, and one of the two major Vishnu-linked forms.
x: Daivathar is one of the two major Vaishnava deities in Theyyam, with Vishnumoorthi. Scholars note that Vaishnavism arrived late in Kerala’s folk religion, so there are few Theyyams in this group. Kerala Tourism says Daivathar stands for Ram

t: The Theyyam that stands for Hanuman in the Ramayana-based group.
x: Bappuran is the third of the linked Ramayana-based Theyyams described by Kerala Tourism, standing for Hanuman. In one telling, the sailor Bappiriyan is also linked to Hanuman, but he is a different Theyyam with a different story.

t: The Chamundi who followed the demons into the underworld.
x: Madayil Chamundi is one of the three well-known forms of Chamundi, with Rakta Chamundi and Kundora Chamundi. She is identified with Kali, who followed the demons she was fighting into the underworld.

t: The Chamundi who fought the demon Darika, and a guardian of village and home.
x: Kundora Chamundi is understood as a fierce form of Kali, and in one reading a partial form of the goddess Kaushiki, who defeated the demon Darika. She is counted among the warrior goddesses and is honoured both as a guardian of the village

t: A goddess linked with Puthiya Bhagavathi, with an unusual story of a divine calf.
x: Padarkulangara is a figure who appears with Puthiya Bhagavathi, according to Kerala Tourism. Sources do not agree on the name. Some write Padarkulangara Bhagavathy and others Padakulangara Veeran, which is a hero rather than a goddess. We f

t: The tigress goddess, daughter of the tiger pair, and the best known of the tiger deities.
x: Puliyoor Kali is the daughter of the tiger deities in the Puli Daivam family and is a tigress goddess. She appears alone in many shrines. When she appears with her mother, the mother is called Valiya Thamburatti and she is Cheriya Thamburat

t: Shiva in tiger form, father of the tiger deities.
x: Pulikandan is the tiger form of Shiva in the story of the Puli Daivam. He is described as a rare Theyyam. A popular source also lists Kandapuli as one of his sons. Sources do not agree on this, and we found no scholarly source.

t: The tigress mother of the tiger deities, known as Valiya Thamburatti.
x: Pulikarinkali is the tigress form of Parvati in the story of the Puli Daivam. When she appears with her daughter Puliyoor Kali, she is called Valiya Thamburatti, the elder lady, and her daughter is Cheriya Thamburatti.

t: A fierce goddess who receives Puthiya Bhagavathi and stays at her side.
x: Veerakali is a fierce goddess who appears with Puthiya Bhagavathi, according to Kerala Tourism. Few sources describe her, and they differ.

t: A goddess of disease and healing, regarded as the younger sister of Puthiya Bhagavathi.
x: Cheerumba Bhagavathi is regarded as the younger sister of Puthiya Bhagavathi. The spelling varies, and so do the stories, as we explain below.

t: A Mappila Theyyam whose figure is Ali, brought before the goddess Chamundi.
x: Aali Theyyam is one of the best-known Mappila Theyyams. Wikipedia says it is kept by members of the Vannan community in the Kumbla area and is linked to the legend of a local family. Names such as Ali Chamundi are also used for it.

t: A mosque officer who became one with the goddess Karinchamundi.
x: Kalanthan Mukri is the Mappila Theyyam at the centre of the best-known Mappila story. A “mukri” is an officer of a mosque. In the festival he appears alongside the Chamundi Theyyam, and Wikipedia says the ritual begins with the call to pray

t: The accompanying Theyyam that becomes Ummachi at the end of its ritual.
x: Yogyar Akampadi is a Theyyam that accompanies Ummachi, according to a Malayalam news report. It is a rare detail, and we found it in only one source.

t: The blood-red Chamundi who drank the blood of Raktabija.
x: Rakta Chamundi is one of the three well-known forms of Chamundi, with Madayil Chamundi and Kundora Chamundi. In the old stories Chamundi is identified with Kali, who killed the demons Chanda and Munda and drank the blood of the demon Raktab

t: A tiger deity, brother of Puliyoor Kali.
x: Puliyoor Kannan is one of the tiger deities in the Puli Daivam family. Popular sources name him as a son of the tiger pair, and a brother of Puliyoor Kali. In some places Puliyoor Kali is said to appear together with him only.

t: A tiger deity, described as a son of Shiva and Parvati in tiger form.
x: Pulimaruthan is a rare tiger Theyyam. Kerala Tourism lists it, and one popular page describes it as a son of Shiva and Parvati in the form of a tiger and tigress. Pulimaranja Thondachan, a different tiger deity, is a separate figure.

t: A tiger deity of the Puli Daivam family.
x: Marapuli is named by Kerala Tourism as one of the tiger Theyyams, and a popular page lists him among the sons of the tiger pair. We found almost nothing else about him.
